models_evaluated: Wizard of Oz simulated pattern-matching chatbot

links.outcome: Knowledge test improvement (high effectiveness group) by technical vs nontechnical reading level of chatbot responses
links.effect: Technical language (grade 12+) responses more likely in high-effectiveness group than nontechnical (grade 8 or below): OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04; participants were college students with high literacy.
links.quote: A binary logistic regression predicting effectiveness ( Table 4 ) revealed that participants who received technical language responses were significantly more likely to be in the high effectiveness group (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P =.04) when compared to participants who received nontechnical language responses.

links.outcome: Effect of plain-language vs technical chatbot responses on learning, trust, and usability
links.effect: Technical language increased effectiveness (OR 2.73) but had no significant effect on trust (OR 0.80, P=.77) or usability (P=.15); sample was college students with relatively high health literacy.
links.quote: Our results found that the chatbot’s responses which used technical language significantly increased the chatbot’s effectiveness but had no impact on trust or usability.

unlisted_practices: Chatbot persona (doctor/nurse/nursing student) design affects usability but not trust or effectiveness

links.effect: Technical language outperformed nontechnical: OR 2.73 (95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04) for high effectiveness.
links.quote: Analysis of 71 participants found that participants who received technical language responses were significantly more likely to be in the high effectiveness group, which had higher improvements in test scores (odds ratio [OR] 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04).

links.effect: Reading level affected effectiveness; technical grade 12+ responses had OR 2.73 (95% CI 1.05-7.41; P=.04) versus nontechnical grade ≤8.
